narrative:
The model estimated a 52.5% probability that you will fail the bar exam on the first try. That is only slightly above even odds, but under the admission rule used, it was enough to lead to rejection. This is a risk estimate, not a certainty about your ability or future performance. Your gender and race were not used in this prediction.

The strongest factor in the decision was your LSAT score. At 32, it was below the average of 37.18 among accepted students, and it was the main factor pushing the prediction toward failure. The second most influential factor was your undergraduate GPA. Your 2.70 is below the accepted-student average of 3.23, but in your case its influence leaned toward passing, so it helped rather than hurt the prediction. The third most influential factor was your third-year academic decile. Your decile of 4 is below the accepted average of 5.79, yet its influence also leaned toward passing. Thus, the rejection was driven most strongly by the LSAT signal, while your GPA and third-year standing softened the result but did not offset it.

To improve your position, focus first on raising your LSAT through structured preparation and, if possible, a retake. Submit any updated academic records and ask admissions whether an appeal, reconsideration, or feedback is available. If you reapply, choose programs that review applicants holistically and seek advising on how to present your strongest evidence.
